title: Inference vs Training — the KV-cache and the two regimes

claims.subject: training
claims.quote: Training is **compute-bound** — the bottleneck is the sheer number of floating-point operations.

claims.subject: training
claims.quote: During **training**, the model sees the *whole* sequence at once — a prompt and its target, as a dense block of $T$ tokens processed in parallel.

claims.subject: decode
claims.quote: Generation is *autoregressive*: you produce **one token at a time**

claims.subject: attention
claims.quote: Attention is $O(T^2)$ in the naive reading

claims.subject: kv-cache
claims.quote: the cache grows by one key and one value per layer, per head, per new token — **linear** in sequence length

claims.subject: kv-cache
claims.quote: decode stays $O(T)$ rather than $O(T^2)$ per step

claims.subject: kv-cache
claims.value: store keys and values of past tokens instead of recomputing them
claims.quote: the keys and values for each past token are computed *once* and **stored**

claims.subject: 32k-context
claims.quote: A 32k-token context means every decode step reads a 32k-token cache.

claims.subject: flashattention
claims.value: the attention matrix is never materialized in memory
claims.quote: reorders the computation so the attention matrix is never materialized in memory, cutting the memory traffic of the attention itself

claims.subject: paged-attention
claims.value: manages the KV-cache in fixed-size blocks like virtual memory
claims.quote: manages the KV-cache like an operating system manages virtual memory — in fixed-size *blocks*

claims.subject: continuous-batching
claims.quote: Continuous batching interleaves many sequences' decode steps

statements.quote: Training and inference are the *same function* — the same weights, the same attention, the same layers — but they are **different forms of computation**, and the difference is the load-bearing fact of the whole serving economy.
In [Attention](attentionlab.php) you saw the mechanism; in [Inference optimization](inference_optimization.php) and [Production serving](production_serving.php) you will meet the tricks.

This chapter gives them the *reason*: why a model that took minutes to train on a batch takes *seconds per token* to serve, and why "how many tokens per second?" and "how many users at once?" are two different questions with two different answers.

blocks.quote: That cache is also, quietly, the most important *physical* object in serving. It is where the memory goes as context length grows, and it is the thing the memory-bound decode step has to move. Everything below — why long contexts are expensive, why people quantize, why they build PagedAttention — is a consequence of that cache.

blocks.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

blocks.quote: Because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, its cost is dominated by *how many bytes you read*, not how many flops you do. And you read two things: the model weights (once per step) and the KV-cache (which grows with context). Three consequences follow, and they shape the entire serving industry (\cite[Pope et al., 2022]{pope2022scaling}).
blocks.section: Why the two regimes set the economics

blocks.quote: > The reason the "optimizations" in the next chapters work is the reason a single token takes as long as it does: inference is not a smaller version of training. It is a *different bottleneck* — one where moving bytes, not computing them, is the scarce resource, and where a linearly growing cache is the object of all the attention.
